title: Using R and Python Together
text:
This post demonstrates how R and Python can be used together in a single Quarto document.
I first calculate average penguin body mass by species in R, pass that result to Python, convert the averages from grams to kilograms in Python, and then pass the result back to R.
Data: Palmer Penguins
Citation: Horst, A. M., Hill, A. P., & Gorman, K. B. (2020). palmerpenguins: Palmer Archipelago (Antarctica) penguin data. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3960218

title: Using R and Python Together
section: Calculate average body mass in R
text:
Calculate average body mass in R

library(palmerpenguins)
library(dplyr)
library(reticulate)

species_mass <- penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    mean_mass_g = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

species_mass

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  species   mean_mass_g
  <fct>           <dbl>
1 Adelie          3701.
2 Chinstrap       3733.
3 Gentoo          5076.


R calculates the average body mass of each penguin species in grams.

title: Using R and Python Together
section: Pass the R result to Python
text:
Pass the R result to Python
The R object species_mass can be accessed from Python using r.species_mass.

species_mass_python = r.species_mass

species_mass_python["mean_mass_kg"] = (
    species_mass_python["mean_mass_g"] / 1000
)

species_mass_python

     species  mean_mass_g  mean_mass_kg
0     Adelie  3700.662252      3.700662
1  Chinstrap  3733.088235      3.733088
2     Gentoo  5076.016260      5.076016


Python receives the result computed in R and adds a new column containing the average body mass in kilograms.

title: Using R and Python Together
section: Pass the Python result back to R
text:
Pass the Python result back to R
The Python object can now be accessed from R using py$species_mass_python.

final_table <- py$species_mass_python

final_table

    species mean_mass_g mean_mass_kg
1    Adelie    3700.662     3.700662
2 Chinstrap    3733.088     3.733088
3    Gentoo    5076.016     5.076016


The final table was therefore produced through both languages: R calculated the original summary, Python transformed it, and R retrieved the transformed result.

title: Penguin Body Mass by Species
text: This post will explore the Palmer Penguins dataset using R.

title: Penguin Body Mass by Species
text:
Data source
Data: Palmer Penguins
The dataset contains measurements of Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo penguins from the Palmer Archipelago in Antarctica. The data are available under a CC0 licence.
Citation: Horst, A. M., Hill, A. P., & Gorman, K. B. (2020). palmerpenguins: Palmer Archipelago (Antarctica) penguin data. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3960218

title: Penguin Body Mass by Species
text:
Load the data

library(palmerpenguins)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

penguins_data <- penguins

head(penguins_data)

# A tibble: 6 × 8
  species island    bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g
  <fct>   <fct>              <dbl>         <dbl>             <int>       <int>
1 Adelie  Torgersen           39.1          18.7               181        3750
2 Adelie  Torgersen           39.5          17.4               186        3800
3 Adelie  Torgersen           40.3          18                 195        3250
4 Adelie  Torgersen           NA            NA                  NA          NA
5 Adelie  Torgersen           36.7          19.3               193        3450
6 Adelie  Torgersen           39.3          20.6               190        3650
# ℹ 2 more variables: sex <fct>, year <int>


The first few rows show that the dataset contains information such as species, island, bill length and depth, flipper length, body mass, sex, and year. It also has 344 records.

title: Penguin Body Mass by Species
text:
Sex distribution across years
Next, I examine whether the distribution of male and female penguins changes across the years represented in the dataset.

sex_distribution <- penguins_data |>
  filter(!is.na(sex)) |>
  count(year, sex)

sex_distribution

# A tibble: 6 × 3
   year sex        n
  <int> <fct>  <int>
1  2007 female    51
2  2007 male      52
3  2008 female    56
4  2008 male      57
5  2009 female    58
6  2009 male      59


This table shows the number of male and female penguins recorded in each year. We can also see that there are records throughout 3 years: 2007, 2008, and 2009
To make comparisons across years easier, I also calculate the proportion of each sex within each year.

sex_proportion <- sex_distribution |>
  group_by(year) |>
  mutate(
    proportion = n / sum(n)
  )

sex_proportion

# A tibble: 6 × 4
# Groups:   year [3]
   year sex        n proportion
  <int> <fct>  <int>      <dbl>
1  2007 female    51      0.495
2  2007 male      52      0.505
3  2008 female    56      0.496
4  2008 male      57      0.504
5  2009 female    58      0.496
6  2009 male      59      0.504


The proportions make it easier to compare the sex distribution across years even when the total number of observations is different.
The male and female proportions remain fairly balanced overall with slight changes from year to year.

title: Penguin Body Mass by Species
text:
Compare species
Next, I calculate the average body mass and flipper length for each species.

species_summary <- penguins_data |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    average_body_mass_g = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
    average_flipper_length_mm = mean(flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    number_of_penguins = n()
  )

species_summary

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  species   average_body_mass_g average_flipper_length_mm number_of_penguins
  <fct>                   <dbl>                     <dbl>              <int>
1 Adelie                  3701.                      190.                152
2 Chinstrap               3733.                      196.                 68
3 Gentoo                  5076.                      217.                124


The summary shows clear differences among the three species.
Gentoo penguins have the highest average body mass and the longest average flipper length. Adelie penguins are generally smaller, while Chinstrap penguins fall between the other two species for several measurements.

title: Penguin Body Mass by Species
section: Relationship between bill length and body mass
text:
Relationship between bill length and body mass
From the average table above, we can see that there might be a correlation between penguins’ measurements. Here, I will examine the relationship between bill length and body mass though a scatterplot.

penguins_original <- ggplot(
  data = penguins,
  mapping = aes(
    x = bill_length_mm,
    y = body_mass_g,
    colour = species
  )
) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  xlab("Bill length (mm)") +
  ylab("Body mass (g)") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(text = element_text(size = 18))

penguins_original

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).








Figure 1: Relationship between bill length and body mass for the three Palmer penguin species.





The scatter plot shows that the three species form distinct groups.
Gentoo penguins generally have greater body mass, while Chinstrap and Adelie penguins tend to have lower body mass. Bill length also differs across species.
Within each species, there appears to be some positive relationship between bill length and body mass, although the strength of the relationship varies with Chinstrap seems to have the weakest relationship.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
My first week in the MDS program was both exciting and very informative. The orientation days covered almost every aspect of the program, from the overall structure and academic expectations to students’ physical and mental well-being, as well as career opportunities after graduation. I also found the IT helpdesk hours very useful, especially for getting everything set up at the beginning.
At the same time, the first week felt a little overwhelming. There were many classes, deadlines, worksheets, lab submissions, and new tools to keep track of, so it took some time to adjust to the pace of the program.
Fortunately, the instructors and TAs have been very helpful and approachable whenever I had questions. Although there is still a lot to get used to, I am starting to become more familiar with the workload and how the program is organized.



Orientation day on campus.

section: Relationship between bill length and body mass
text:
Relationship between bill length and body mass
From the average table above, we can see that there might be a correlation between penguins’ measurements. Here, I will examine the relationship between bill length and body mass though a scatterplot.

for species in penguins["species"].dropna().unique():
    subset = penguins[penguins["species"] == species]

    plt.scatter(
        subset["bill_length_mm"],
        subset["body_mass_g"],
        label=species,
        s=40
    )

plt.xlabel("Bill length (mm)")
plt.ylabel("Body mass (g)")
plt.legend(title="Species")
plt.show()







Figure 1: Relationship between bill length and body mass for the three Palmer penguin species.





The scatter plot shows that the three species form distinct groups.
Gentoo penguins generally have greater body mass, while Chinstrap and Adelie penguins tend to have lower body mass. Bill length also differs across species.
Within each species, there appears to be some positive relationship between bill length and body mass, although the strength of the relationship varies with Chinstrap seems to have the weakest relationship.
